title: NASA Invites ISRO to Join Its Lunar Base Programme Under Expanded Artemis Partnership
excerpt: At the 9th Civil Space Joint Working Group in Bengaluru, NASA formally invited India's space agency to participate in the Moon Base initiative, deepening an already historic collaboration.
body:
• NASA has formally invited ISRO to participate in its Moon Base programme during the 9th Civil Space Joint Working Group (CSJWG) meeting in Bengaluru
  • The invitation falls under the TRUST (Technology, Research, and Understanding for Space Cooperation) initiative within the broader Artemis Accords framework
  • India and the US are already collaborating on the NISAR earth observation satellite, set to launch in 2026
  • The partnership positions India as a key player in humanity's return to the Moon, building on the success of Chandrayaan-3

From Chandrayaan to the Moon Base

NASA has formally invited India's space agency ISRO to join its Moon Base programme, a significant expansion of the growing space partnership between the world's two largest democracies. The invitation was extended during the 9th meeting of the US-India Civil Space Joint Working Group, held in Bengaluru on August 11.

https://x.com/imRavikantYadav/status/2089655394516054404

The Moon Base programme falls under NASA's TRUST initiative — Technology, Research, and Understanding for Space Cooperation — which itself operates within the broader Artemis Accords framework that India signed in 2023. The invitation positions ISRO as a potential contributor to the infrastructure that will support sustained human presence on the lunar surface.

For India, the invitation represents a remarkable trajectory. Just three years ago, ISRO's Chandrayaan-3 mission made India the fourth country to successfully land on the Moon and the first to land near the lunar south pole. That achievement, celebrated across the global Indian diaspora, transformed India's standing in the international space community from a capable but budget-focused programme to a serious partner for the most ambitious missions in human spaceflight.

What the Partnership Looks Like

The details of India's potential contribution to the Moon Base remain under discussion, but the CSJWG meeting covered several areas of collaboration. These include lunar surface operations, space situational awareness, and earth observation — the last of which is already producing tangible results through the joint NASA-ISRO Synthetic Aperture Radar satellite, known as NISAR.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=02_BDVPuxEY

"The CSJWG meeting explored new avenues for cooperation including lunar surface activities, space situational awareness, and earth science applications."

— Joint statement, 9th CSJWG

NISAR, which has been in development for nearly a decade, is scheduled for launch in 2026 and will map the entire globe every 12 days, tracking changes in ecosystems, ice masses, and geological hazards with unprecedented precision. It represents the most significant joint engineering project between the two space agencies to date.

The Broader Geopolitical Picture

NASA's outreach to ISRO is not happening in a vacuum. The Artemis programme is as much a geopolitical project as a scientific one, designed to establish a US-led framework for lunar exploration that serves as an alternative to China's growing space ambitions. China and Russia have announced their own International Lunar Research Station programme, and both countries have been actively courting partners across Asia and Africa.

India's participation in the Artemis framework is diplomatically significant. New Delhi has historically maintained a non-aligned posture in space cooperation, working with both NASA and Roscosmos. Its decision to sign the Artemis Accords — and now deepen that commitment through the Moon Base programme — reflects a broader strategic tilt toward the United States that has accelerated under the Modi government.

Opportunities for Indian-American Scientists

For the estimated 300,000 Indian-origin scientists and engineers working in the US technology and aerospace sectors, the deepening NASA-ISRO partnership opens intriguing possibilities. Joint missions create pathways for cross-pollination between American and Indian research institutions, and could eventually lead to Indian astronauts participating in lunar surface missions under the Artemis umbrella.

ISRO's inclusion in the Moon Base programme also reinforces a narrative that resonates powerfully in the diaspora: that India is no longer just reaching for the stars on a budget, but standing alongside the world's leading space power as an equal partner in exploring them.
